```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.5)
```

```{r setup}
library(isoniche)
```

Isodars are estimated from the spread of a species' densities across
replicates, so a species needs enough replicates, enough individuals and a
consistent habitat preference for its niche breadth to be estimated well.
Many species in a typical community data set will not meet these
requirements. `niche_breadth()` never stops on such a species: it returns
an estimate where it can, and records each potential problem as a logical
`flag_*` column. This vignette explains each flag and what to do about it.

## All species of the Moorea data

```{r all}
nb <- niche_breadth(moorea_fish, species = "species", site = "site",
                    habitat = "habitat", abundance = "abundance",
                    n_boot = 0, seed = 1)
summary(nb)
```

In a data set of 13 sites, most rare species cannot be analysed. This is
expected: the same species would also give unreliable classic niche breadth
values, but without any warning.

## The flags

Thresholds are arguments of `niche_breadth()`, set through `diagnostics`
(e.g. `diagnostics = list(min_sites = 8)`); the defaults are given below.

### Data

* **`few_sites`**: fewer than `min_sites` (10) replicates with the species.
  Isodars from few points are imprecise. Group nearby sites
  (`group_sites()`; see `vignette("data-preparation")`) or treat the species
  as unreliable.
* **`few_pair_sites`**: some pair of used habitats was sampled together at
  fewer than `min_pair_sites` (5) sites, so its pairwise isodar is poorly
  estimated. Use the n-dimensional isodar with `ndim_method = "latent"`, or
  group sites.
* **`low_abundance`**: the median site total is below `min_median_count` (5)
  individuals, or more than `max_zero_share` (half) of the counts in used
  habitats are zeros. Densities are then dominated by sampling noise.
* **`undersampled`**: a habitat without records was sampled at too few sites
  to call it absent. Sample more sites, or decide on ecological grounds and
  name absent habitats with `absent`.

### Fit

* **`fit_failed`**: the isodars could not be fitted; the reason is in the
  `note` column. Most often the species has too few sites.
* **`disconnected`**: some habitats never occur together at a site, so their
  relationship cannot be estimated.
* **`poor_fit`**: for the n-dimensional isodar, the line explains less than
  `min_var_explained` (50%) of the variance; for pairwise isodars, the
  isodars of three habitats contradict each other (the product of two slopes
  differs from the third by more than a factor `max_slope_ratio`, 2, or in
  sign). Habitat selection may not follow a single isodar, or the data are
  too noisy. Look at the isodars with `fit_isodars()`, and try the other
  method (`dim = "ndim"` or `"pairwise"`).
* **`no_di`**: no total abundance up to `max_search` puts an individual in
  every used habitat: the least-favoured habitat is predicted never to fill.
* **`intercept_noise`**: the isodar intercepts do not differ from those
  expected by sampling alone (see below). The data then give no evidence
  that niche breadth changes with abundance: with zero intercepts, the
  isodars pass through the origin and DI and DD niche breadth are equal.
  Report a single value, DD niche breadth, which rests on the slopes only
  and is the better estimated. With few sites the test has little power, so
  this flag does not show that the intercepts are zero.

### Extrapolation

* **`di_extrapolation`**: the spillover abundance lies outside the observed
  range of site totals by more than a factor `extrapolation_ratio` (2).
* **`dd_extrapolation`**: the largest site total is below twice the
  spillover abundance, so the data never reach the halfway point of the
  curve towards DD niche breadth.

Both are extrapolations of the fitted isodars; the estimates may be right,
but rest on the assumption that the isodars hold beyond the data.

### Uncertainty

* **`unstable_bootstrap`** (only with `n_boot > 0`): more than
  `max_failed_share` (10%) of bootstrap replicates failed, or a confidence
  interval is wider than `max_ci_width` (0.5). Increase `n_boot`; if the
  interval stays wide, the data cannot resolve the species' niche breadth.

### Informational

* **`reversal`**: two habitats swap rank as abundance increases; the
  abundances are in the `reversals` column. Niche breadth can then change
  non-monotonically with abundance, so compare species at a stated
  abundance.
* **`abandoned`**: a habitat used at low abundance is predicted to be empty
  at high abundance; it counts for DI but not DD niche breadth.

## Is the intercept more than noise?

When a species is rare, counts in its habitats are small and their ratios
noisy, which alone produces isodar intercepts. `niche_breadth()` tests
whether the observed intercepts exceed this: it simulates `n_null` (199)
data sets in which each site's individuals are redistributed among its
habitats at random, in proportion to the species' overall density in each
habitat (no density dependence), refits the isodars, and compares the
observed intercepts with the simulated ones. `intercept_p` is the smallest
Holm-corrected p-value; the species is flagged when it exceeds `alpha`
(0.05). The test needs integer counts.

```{r noise}
noisy <- nb[nb$flag_intercept_noise & !nb$flag_few_sites, ]
noisy[c("species", "nb_di", "nb_dd", "intercept_p")]
```

## Looking at a flagged species

Diagnostics are a starting point. For a flagged species, look at its
isodars and curve:

```{r look}
sp <- "Acanthurus nigrofuscus"
nb[nb$species == sp, c("nb_di", "nb_dd", "var_explained", "flags")]
fit <- fit_isodars(moorea_fish[moorea_fish$species == sp, ], site = "site",
                   habitat = "habitat", abundance = "abundance")
fit$fit[[1]]
```

```{r look-curve, fig.height = 5}
plot(iai_curve(fit))
nb$reversals[[which(nb$species == sp)]]
```

When rare, this species lives on the fringing and barrier reefs: both
isodars against the outer slope have large intercepts. But the outer slope
fills fastest as abundance rises (the reefs gain only 0.27 and 0.08
individuals per individual on the outer slope), so it overtakes both reefs
at a few hundred individuals, the ranking of habitats changes and niche
breadth first rises, then falls. Here the pairwise isodars are also
somewhat inconsistent with each other (`poor_fit`). Neither DI nor DD niche
breadth alone describes such a species well; the curve does.

## A workflow

1. Run `check_coverage()` and drop species or habitats that are clearly
   undersampled.
2. Run `niche_breadth()` with `n_boot = 0` on all species; look at
   `summary()`.
3. Decide how to handle each warning flag (for example: drop species with
   `fit_failed`, `few_sites` or `low_abundance`; report DI and DD niche
   breadth separately only where `intercept_noise` is not raised).
4. Rerun on the retained species with `n_boot = 999` or more, and check
   `unstable_bootstrap`.
5. Report the thresholds and how many species each rule removed.
